questions.prompt: One Gauss-Newton step on a residual \(r(x)\) does which of the following?
options: Replace \(r\) by the linear model \(r + J_r d\) and solve that linear least-squares problem for \(d\).
Set \(r(x) = 0\) by inspection and stop, without using a Jacobian.
Replace \(r\) by the Hessian of \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) and stop.
Step in a direction orthogonal to every row of the Jacobian.
questions.explanation: The linear model of the residual is \(r(x) + J_r(x)\, d\). Gauss-Newton chooses \(d\) to minimize the norm of that model, which is a linear least-squares problem with normal equations \(J_r^T J_r\, d = -J_r^T r\). Setting the nonlinear residual to zero is the goal of the iteration, not one step. The Hessian of the sum of squares is a different matrix, and it is not what this step solves. A direction orthogonal to every Jacobian row has a zero first-order change in the residual, so it is not the least-squares step.

questions.prompt: The residual is \(r(t) = (t - 1,\ 2t - 4)\). At \(t = 0\), what is the Gauss-Newton step \(d\) in \(t\)?
questions.explanation: At \(t = 0\) the residual is \((-1, -4)\) and the Jacobian column is \((1, 2)\). Then \(J^T J = 1 + 4 = 5\) and \(J^T r = -1 - 8 = -9\), so \(5d = 9\) and \(d = 9/5 = 1.8\). The residual is affine, so this one step is the exact least-squares fit. Reporting \(9\) skips the division by the Gram entry. Reporting \(-1.8\) flips the normal equation. Reporting \(5\) is \(J^T J\) itself, not the step.

questions.prompt: The Gauss-Newton matrix \(J_r^T J_r\) equals the true Hessian of \(f = \tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) when
options: the Jacobian is singular
the step length is shorter than one
the residual is nonlinear and nonzero
every residual component is affine, or the residual vector is zero
questions.explanation: The true Hessian is \(J_r^T J_r + \sum_i r_i \nabla^2 r_i\). Each second-derivative term vanishes when that component is affine, and the whole sum vanishes when \(r = 0\). A singular Jacobian does not cancel those terms. A short step is a line-search choice and does not change the Hessian. A nonlinear nonzero residual is exactly the case where the extra term can be nonzero, so the two matrices differ.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one Gauss-Newton iteration in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The residual and the Jacobian have to be known before the normal equations can be written. The equations have to be written before they can be solved. The point moves only after the step is in hand. Solving a model built at the new point would be the next iteration, not this one.

steps: Evaluate the residual \(r\) and its Jacobian \(J_r\) at the current point.
Form the normal equations \(J_r^T J_r\, d = -J_r^T r\) of the linearized residual.
Solve those equations for the step \(d\).
Replace the current point by the point plus \(d\).

questions.prompt: Which statements about a Gauss-Newton step are true?
options: The step minimizes the norm of the linearized residual.
If \(J_r\) has full column rank and \(J_r^T r \ne 0\), the step is a descent direction for \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\).
\(J_r^T J_r\) is positive semidefinite for every real Jacobian.
The linear model keeps the second derivatives of the residual components.
One step reaches a root of every nonlinear residual.
questions.explanation:
The normal equations are the stationarity condition for the linear least-squares model, so the step minimizes that model.
• Full column rank makes \(J_r^T J_r\) positive definite. The directional derivative of \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) along the step is then \(-(J_r^T r)^T (J_r^T J_r)^{-1} (J_r^T r)\), which is negative when the gradient is not zero.
• For every real matrix, \(v^T J_r^T J_r v = \lVert J_r v\rVert^2 \ge 0\), so the Gram matrix is positive semidefinite even when it is singular.
• Second derivatives of the components are exactly the terms Gauss-Newton drops. At \(u = 2\) for \(r(u) = (u^2 - 10,\ 2u - 4)\), that dropped term equals \(-12\), and the true Hessian is \(8\) rather than \(J^T J = 20\).
• The same point moves by \(1.2\), and the nonlinear residual there is \((0.24,\ 2.4)\), not zero.

questions.prompt: A scalar parameter has residual entries \(a\) and \(b\), with Jacobian entries \(p\) and \(q\). The Gauss-Newton step equals
questions.explanation: The Gram entry is \(p^2 + q^2\) and the right-hand side of the normal equation is \(-(pa + qb)\), so the step is \(-(pa + qb)/(p^2 + q^2)\). Every declared name appears: \(a\) and \(b\) are the residual entries, and \(p\) and \(q\) are the Jacobian entries. Dropping the minus sign climbs the residual model. Using \(p^2 + q^2\) in the numerator swaps the Gram matrix with the gradient. Replacing the denominator by \(p + q\) adds the rows instead of squaring them.

questions.prompt: A note computes a Gauss-Newton step for \(r(x) = (x^2 - 5,\ x - 1)\) at \(x = 2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The residual \((4 - 5,\ 2 - 1) = (-1,\ 1)\) is correct. Differentiating \(x^2\) produces \(2x\), so the Jacobian at \(2\) is \((4,\ 1)\), and \(4^2 + 1^2 = 17\), \(4\cdot(-1) + 1 = -3\), and the step is \(3/17\). The false step replaces \(2x\) by \(x\). That is a different linear model, and the normal equations built from \((2,\ 1)\) are not the Gauss-Newton step.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
steps: The derivative of \(x^2 - 5\) is \(2x\), so the Jacobian at \(2\) is \((4,\ 1)\).
The derivative of \(x^2 - 5\) may be replaced by \(x\), so the Jacobian at \(2\) is \((2,\ 1)\).
With the Jacobian \((4,\ 1)\), one has \(J^T J = 17\) and \(J^T r = -3\), so the step is \(3/17\).
reasons: The derivative of \(x^2\) is \(2x\), so the Jacobian at \(2\) is \((4,\ 1)\), not \((2,\ 1)\).
For the Jacobian \((4,\ 1)\), the product \(J^T J\) is not \(17\).

questions.prompt: The residual is \(r(u) = (u^2 - 10,\ 2u - 4)\). At \(u = 2\), what is the Gauss-Newton step \(d\)?
questions.explanation: The residual is \((-6,\ 0)\) and the Jacobian column is \((4,\ 2)\). Then \(J^T J = 16 + 4 = 20\) and \(J^T r = -24\), so \(d = 24/20 = 1.2\). Reporting \(24\) skips the division. Reporting \(-1.2\) flips the sign of the normal equation. Reporting \(20\) is the Gram entry. The updated parameter would be \(3.2\), which is the point plus the step, not the step itself.

questions.prompt: At \(u = 2\) for \(r(u) = (u^2 - 10,\ 2u - 4)\), the true Hessian of \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) and the Gauss-Newton matrix differ because
options: \(J^T J\) is indefinite
the second residual component is zero, which removes \(J^T J\)
the first residual is \(-6\) and its second derivative is \(2\), which contributes \(-12\)
the Jacobian column \((4,\ 2)\) is orthogonal to the residual
questions.explanation: The extra Hessian term is \(\sum_i r_i\) times the second derivative of component \(i\). Here that is \((-6)\cdot 2 + 0 = -12\). Added to \(J^T J = 20\), the true Hessian is \(8\). The Jacobian is not orthogonal to the residual: their dot product is \(-24\). A Gram matrix is positive semidefinite, and here it equals \(20\), so it is not indefinite. A zero residual component drops that component's second-derivative term; it does not drop \(J^T J\).

questions.prompt: When \(J_r^T J_r\) is nearly singular, the plain Gauss-Newton step can be very long. The method that adds a positive multiple of the identity before solving is
options: a spectral decomposition of the residual
a damped Gauss-Newton step
a simplex pivot on a linear program
an exact line search that ignores the Jacobian
questions.explanation: Adding \(\mu I\) with \(\mu > 0\) is the damped step. The shift makes the matrix positive definite, and a large \(\mu\) shortens the step toward steepest descent. A simplex pivot is a basis change for a linear program. An exact line search still needs a direction, and dropping the Jacobian removes the least-squares model. A spectral decomposition reads eigenvalues; it does not build the step.

questions.prompt: For \(r(u) = (u^2 - 10,\ 2u - 4)\) at \(u = 2\), the Gauss-Newton step is \(1.2\) and \(J^T r = -24\). What is the directional derivative of \(f = \tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) along that step?
questions.explanation: The gradient of \(f\) is \(J^T r = -24\). Along \(d = 1.2\) the directional derivative is \(-24 \cdot 1.2 = -28.8\). The negative sign is what makes the step a descent direction. Reporting \(28.8\) drops that sign. Reporting \(-24\) is the gradient, not its product with the step. Reporting \(1.2\) is the step length.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: On a residual that is already affine, one Gauss-Newton step is exact. Applying that step to the old quadratic plus one new linear block is the optimization view of
options: the measurement update of a linear recursive least-squares fit
a phase-one simplex iteration
an Armijo test with no residual
a power iteration for the largest eigenvalue
questions.explanation: A linear residual makes one Gauss-Newton step exact for the cost it is given. Recursive least squares gives it the old quadratic plus the new block, not the new block by itself, and that step is the Kalman measurement update. A phase-one iteration introduces artificial variables for a linear program. Armijo is a sufficient-decrease test on a step that has already been chosen. Power iteration multiplies by a matrix to find an eigenvector.
